newsitem.title: USA: Florida to seek $12.3 billion verdict in tobacco case.
newsitem.headline: Florida to seek $12.3 billion verdict in tobacco case.

text.p: A lawyer for Florida said on Monday the state would ask jurors for $12.3 billion in damages against cigarette companies in its landmark case against the tobacco industry.

"Are you offended by a number like this?" Robert Montgomery asked in remarks to potential jurors in the case, the first state lawsuit seeking to recoup costs of treating smoking-related illnesses to go to trial. Opening statements are expected to begin shortly after Labor Day.

Standing before 36 jury candidates, Montgomery began what he called the "most tedious time of a lawsuit," jury selection. On Tuesday the same prospective jurors will be questioned by tobacco company lawyers.

Palm Beach County Circuit Court Judge Harold Cohen has set this week for screening out prospective jurors with opinions so deep-seated they could not reach a fair verdict. Cohen said he hoped the lawyers would choose six jurors and nine alternates starting next week.

But finding suitable jurors is proving to be no easy task as Montgomery found when one Palm Beach County schoolteacher told the court there was no way "I could be fair" in rendering a verdict that included punitive damages.

Kathryn Neiswender said she would have no problem in awarding Florida $1.3 billion if the state proves its case. Florida is seeking reimbursement for treating smoking-related illnesses under the state and federal Medicaid insurance plan.
But she said she did have problem in awarding $11 billion to the state for punitive damages without knowing what the state planned to do with the money.
"I would be concerned with how that money ($11 billion) would be dispensed," said Neiswender, who eventually was dismissed as a potential juror.
Another potential juror, Michael Kirk, explained he was concerned about the addiction issue.
"Since I was 13 years old, virtually every member of the family has been touched by cancer (related to their smoking)," he said.
"My grandfather died of lung cancer, my father died of lung cancer, and (only four weeks ago) my brother-in-law died of brain and lung cancer," he said, choking back tears.
Kirk, whose wife has been unable to quit smoking despite her husband's urging, said the deaths would affect his ability to render the "fair and impartial verdict" that Montgomery said he was seeking.
Montgomery said the state would seek $12.3 billion in compensatory and punitive damages.
